final_answer:
A stack and a queue are both linear data structures, but they differ in how elements are added and removed. A **stack** follows the **Last-In-First-Out (LIFO)** principle, meaning the last element added is the first to be removed. Operations occur at one end, called the "top." A **queue** follows the **First-In-First-Out (FIFO)** principle, where the first element added is the first to be removed. Elements are added at the "rear" and removed from the "front." 

A real-world example of a **stack** is a browser's back button. When navigating through web pages, each new page is pushed onto the stack. Clicking the back button pops the most recent page, adhering to the LIFO principle. 

A real-world example of a **queue** is a printer queue. When multiple documents are sent to a printer, they are added to the queue in the order received. The printer processes documents in the same order, reflecting the FIFO behavior of a queue.
